strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem in 3D vision: systematically determining the design principles and parameters that make synthetic training datasets effective for zero-shot stereo matching.

Provides extensive and well-controlled empirical ablations across multiple generation parameters, including floating object density, background presence, object/material diversity, camera baseline distributions, lighting augmentations, and ray-tracing sample fidelity.

Presents critical practical optimizations for dataset generation (e.g., greedy solver for room generation and OptiX denoising with reduced ray-tracing samples) that reduce CPU and GPU compute by factors of ~3.9x and ~7.5x respectively, making procedural data generation practically accessible.

Demonstrates strong empirical performance: models trained exclusively on Infinigen-Stereo-150k outperform models trained on existing synthetic datasets (SceneFlow, CREStereo, TartanAir, IRS) individually as well as their 600k combined mixture, showing remarkable sample efficiency and robust zero-shot cross-dataset generalization across Middlebury, ETH3D, KITTI, and Booster.
The commitment to open-source the procedural generator and pipeline represents a valuable resource for reproducible research and further domain customization in stereo vision.
weaknesses: The architectural diversity in the ablation study is somewhat limited; all design parameter ablations are conducted solely using RAFT-Stereo, leaving open whether some specific procedural choices interact differently with distinct architectures (e.g., cost-volume/3D CNN-based architectures like PSMNet).

The paper strictly focuses on zero-shot generalization and does not evaluate downstream fine-tuning performance (e.g., testing whether pre-training on Infinigen-Stereo improves final benchmark leaderboard results when fine-tuned on KITTI or Middlebury relative to standard SceneFlow pre-training).

Evaluation in Tables 1-4 primarily reports outlier pixel percentages (>2px or >3px error); including standard End-Point Error (EPE) metrics alongside bad-pixel percentages across all benchmarks would provide a more complete assessment of subpixel precision.

strengths: Systematic and insightful exploration of the procedural design space for 3D stereo matching datasets, addressing a long-standing question that was previously mostly explored for 2D optical flow (e.g., Mayer et al., 2018).

Thorough parameter ablation studies in Section 3 (Table 1 and Table 2), evaluating object density, background inclusion, object/material filtering, stereo baseline distributions, ray-tracing quality, and scene-type mixtures across multiple standard benchmarks (Middlebury, ETH3D, KITTI, Booster).

Practical computational optimization of procedural generation: significantly reducing CPU scene solving time (3.9x) and GPU rendering time (7.5x via OptiX denoising) without sacrificing downstream stereo performance.

Strong zero-shot performance and sample efficiency: models trained solely on Infinigen-Stereo-150k outperform prior checkpoints and models trained on a 600k combination of SceneFlow, CREStereo, TartanAir, and IRS by noticeable margins, while showing superior sample scaling.
weaknesses: Ablations in Table 1 are conducted at a relatively small scale (5k pairs, 75k iterations) with a single architecture (RAFT-Stereo). While understandable due to compute limits, it remains unverified whether some observed behaviors (e.g., lighting variation having negligible impact, or specific object category effects) generalize at full scale or across fundamentally different stereo architectures (such as 3D CNN / cost-volume based networks like PSMNet or GMStereo).

The evaluation is restricted entirely to zero-shot generalization. Demonstrating whether pre-training on Infinigen-Stereo-150k also yields gains when fine-tuned on target datasets (e.g., official KITTI and Middlebury benchmark leaderboards) relative to standard SceneFlow pre-training would provide a more complete picture of its utility as a foundational stereo dataset.

strengths: Comprehensive and systematic empirical study: The paper presents an extensive investigation into the design space of 3D synthetic stereo datasets (e.g., floating object density, arrangement realism, baseline distribution, material properties, and ray-tracing noise), addressing an important gap in modern 3D stereo dataset literature.

Significant zero-shot performance gains: Models trained solely on Infinigen-Stereo-150k outperform existing off-the-shelf checkpoints and baselines trained on a combination of 600k samples from standard datasets (SceneFlow, CREStereo, TartanAir, IRS) across multiple benchmark suites (Middlebury 2014/2021, ETH3D, KITTI 2012/2015, and Booster).

Effective computational optimizations: The authors provide practical engineering solutions to the severe computational bottlenecks of procedural generation (e.g., greedy indoor layout solver, camera placement amortization, and OptiX denoising with reduced sample count), reducing generation overhead substantially while preserving downstream utility.

Strong sample efficiency: The analysis demonstrates remarkable sample efficiency (Fig. 6), where 500 samples from the proposed distribution outperform orders of magnitude more samples from legacy synthetic datasets.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is limited: The methodology relies predominantly on engineering and tuning existing platforms (Infinigen Indoors/Nature and Blender Cycles) rather than proposing a fundamentally novel generative paradigm or automated parameter optimization framework (e.g., bilevel optimization as in AutoFlow).

Ad-hoc manual curation: Several key parameter and asset choices (such as removing specific objects like cacti/urchins and eliminating certain glass/specular materials) rely on post-hoc manual inspection rather than principled or automated curriculum learning.

Lack of fine-tuning benchmarks: The evaluation focuses exclusively on zero-shot generalization; demonstrating whether pre-training on Infinigen-Stereo provides superior initialization when fine-tuning on benchmark training sets (e.g., KITTI benchmark leaderboard protocols) would strengthen the empirical claims.

Removal of difficult surface phenomena: Completely pruning troublesome non-Lambertian surfaces (extreme glass/mirrors) to stabilize training may limit the network's capacity to handle complex in-the-wild specularities, even if it improves aggregate benchmark metrics.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored question in stereo matching: systematically decomposing and analyzing which factors in procedural synthetic data generation contribute to strong zero-shot real-world generalization.

Provides extensive, well-structured empirical ablations across multiple procedural parameters, including floating object density, background realism, object categories, materials, stereo baseline diversity, lighting, and scene type distributions.

Carefully considers the practical computation costs of procedural generation, demonstrating effective optimizations (e.g., greedy indoor solvers, OptiX denoising at lower ray samples, camera trajectory amortization) that achieve a ~6x speedup without sacrificing zero-shot downstream utility under fixed compute budgets.

Strong empirical performance: models trained on the resulting WMGStereo-150k dataset substantially outperform models trained on widely used datasets (SceneFlow, CREStereo, TartanAir, IRS, and their combination), exhibit impressive sample efficiency (500 samples rivaling 100k CREStereo samples on Middlebury), and achieve performance competitive with FoundationStereo while releasing an open-source procedural generator.
weaknesses: The parameter ablation study (Tab. 1 and Tab. 3) relies exclusively on a single architecture (RAFT-Stereo) trained on a small budget (5k pairs, 75k steps). While full-scale training validates that final datasets transfer to DLNR and Selective-IGEV, verifying whether specific ablation findings (such as material sensitivity or baseline distributions) generalize equally across different network paradigms (e.g., 3D cost-volume vs. iterative recurrent) would further strengthen the claims.

Although competitive overall, models trained on FoundationStereo Data (FSD) still outperform WMGStereo-150k on several benchmarks (notably Booster and ETH3D in Tab. 5). A deeper analysis into what specific visual/geometric characteristics in FSD drive this remaining performance gap would provide valuable insight.

The generator focuses heavily on indoor rooms and abstract floating objects, with relatively coarse treatment of outdoor/driving scene parameters despite driving benchmarks (KITTI, DrivingStereo) being core evaluation targets.

strengths: Systematic and timely empirical study: While synthetic data is foundational to deep stereo matching, prior work rarely isolated the impact of procedural 3D generation parameters (e.g., floating object density, scene realism vs. random objects, material distributions, baseline variation). This study provides actionable insights into what actually drives zero-shot generalization.

Insightful findings: The discovery that combining realistic background layouts with dense floating foreground objects outperforms either pure realism or pure floating objects provides a concrete recipe for synthetic stereo generation. Additionally, identifying and removing hyper-challenging or ill-posed geometry/materials (such as extremely thin needle structures or fully specular/transparent surfaces) to prevent optimization collapse is practically valuable.

Data generation cost optimization: Infinigen is computationally expensive to run out-of-the-box. The paper provides effective strategies—such as solver step truncation, Blender OptiX denoising at lower ray-tracing sample counts, and multi-rig camera amortization—and validates their efficacy under compute-matched settings.

Strong performance and sample efficiency: Models trained on WMGStereo-150k consistently outperform models trained on a 600k mixture of classical datasets (SceneFlow, CREStereo, TartanAir, IRS) across multiple architectures (RAFT-Stereo, DLNR, Selective-IGEV) on Middlebury, KITTI, and Booster. The sample efficiency demonstrated in Figure 5 (500 samples outperforming 100k CREStereo pairs on Middlebury) is particularly impressive.

Open-source commitment: Providing the procedural dataset generation code and configurations alongside the dataset enables the community to systematically generate targeted variations and build upon this data recipe.
weaknesses: Isolated parameter study without cross-parameter interactions: The parameter study in Section 3 varies one dimension at a time on a fixed subset (5k pairs, 75k iterations) of indoor floating scenes. It leaves open the question of how strong interaction effects might be (e.g., between material complexity and lighting variations, or baseline distributions across different scene densities).

Limited novelty in procedural tooling: Technically, the work heavily leverages existing Infinigen Indoors and Nature assets and Blender APIs, with the main contributions lying in empirical findings, asset pruning heuristics, and placement scripts rather than new rendering or procedural modeling algorithms.

Evaluation on FoundationStereo architecture: While DLNR is benchmarked when trained on WMGStereo-150k versus FSD, the FoundationStereo model architecture itself was not trained on WMGStereo-150k, leaving a small gap in establishing whether the dataset scales equally well to larger transformer-based foundation architectures.

strengths: Comprehensive and systematic parameter study: The paper presents an in-depth empirical exploration of crucial synthetic generation parameters for stereo matching, including object clutter/density, scene layout realism, baseline distributions, material properties, and lighting. This addresses an important question that has previously been handled via ad-hoc heuristics.

Strong and consistent downstream zero-shot generalization: Training on the proposed WMGStereo-150k dataset leads to substantial improvements across standard benchmarks (Middlebury 2014/2021, ETH3D, KITTI 2012/2015, and Booster), consistently outperforming prior widely used datasets (SceneFlow, CREStereo, TartanAir, IRS) and the combined 'Mixed' baseline across multiple architectures (RAFT-Stereo, DLNR, Selective-IGEV).

High sample efficiency: As demonstrated in Fig. 5, models trained on as few as 500 examples from WMGStereo-150k achieve lower end-point error on Middlebury than those trained on 100k CREStereo pairs, showing that the data diversity and composition are well-optimized.

Practical efficiency and cost optimization: Section 3.3 provides valuable analysis on rendering tradeoffs (solver steps, sample count vs. OptiX denoising, camera rig amortizations), achieving a ~6x reduction in data generation cost while preserving downstream model accuracy.

Value to the community: Releasing the procedural generation pipeline and configurations built on top of Infinigen provides an open-source, reproducible alternative to proprietary or non-reproducible datasets such as FoundationStereo's FSD.
weaknesses: Univariate exploration of the design space: The parameter study in Section 3 mostly modifies one variable at a time while holding the rest constant. This one-factor-at-a-time approach may overlook important coupling effects between parameters (e.g., the interaction between material transparency and lighting augmentations, or camera baseline distributions and scene depth ranges).

Limited algorithmic novelty: The work primarily orchestrates and tunes existing procedural generation tools (Infinigen and Blender) rather than introducing new algorithmic generation techniques or stereo architectures.

Some predictable findings: Several conclusions—such as randomized baselines being required to bridge small- and large-baseline benchmarks, or extreme specularities/transparencies degrading diffuse matching accuracy—are already recognized in the stereo matching literature, though the paper still provides welcome empirical confirmation.

Absence of fine-tuning evaluations: The paper focuses exclusively on zero-shot generalization. While this is an important and representative setting, reporting how pre-training on WMGStereo-150k impacts target domain fine-tuning (e.g., standard KITTI or Middlebury benchmark submission protocols) would further strengthen the claims of dataset utility.
